passage:
Supervisor's note, claims team, end of quarter.
I've been part of the problem. Every time something urgent came in this quarter, I gave it to Minakshi, because she always delivers. The clinic audit, the backlog from Swati's leave, the Friday reports: Minakshi. Meanwhile Swati and Rohit left at five most days with half their queues untouched, and nobody asked why.
This week I noticed Minakshi eating lunch at her desk three days running. When I thanked her in the team meeting, she smiled and said, "Happy to help." Later, in the lift, she said quietly, "Sometimes being good at this feels like a punishment." Then she laughed and added that she does like being the one people count on.
What I did next: I moved the Friday reports to Rohit, asked Swati to take back her own backlog, and set time to ask Minakshi what she'd like to hand over, not just what she can carry.

qa.q: Where did Minakshi eat lunch three days running?
qa.a: At her desk.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Minakshi show in the lift?
qa.a: She feels used and worn out, as if being good at the job is a punishment, yet also proud of being the one people count on.

qa.q: Why might the supervisor's changes help Minakshi?
qa.a: Spreading the work back to Swati and Rohit and asking what Minakshi wants to hand over stops her reliability being turned into extra load.

qa.q: How might Rohit react to suddenly getting the Friday reports?
qa.a: Rohit may be surprised or a bit annoyed at first, but it also shows that the uneven effort has finally been noticed.

grounding: Shows a dependable colleague who keeps getting extra work while others coast, feeling both used and proud of being relied on.

passage:
Jaya, you asked how old Jomon handles a team where one person does everything. Let me tell you about my first team, at a printing press in Kochi.
I was twenty-five, managing four people. Susan did the proofs, the layouts, the late-night fixes. Benny chatted with clients and somehow never had a finished page. For months I said nothing. Susan never complained, and Benny made everyone laugh.
Then one evening I found Susan asleep on the paper stacks at nine, and Benny's desk empty since four. That's when I saw it: by keeping quiet, I was paying for Benny's ease with Susan's health.
Next morning I took Benny out for tea, just the two of us. No shouting. I showed him the job sheet and asked, "What's getting in your way?" He went red, then admitted he was scared of the new layout software. Within a month he was doing his share, and Susan finally took her leave.

qa.q: Where was Jomon's first team?
qa.a: At a printing press in Kochi.

qa.q: What did young Jomon feel on finding Susan asleep on the paper stacks?
qa.a: Jomon felt a jolt of guilt and alarm, realising that months of silence had been costing Susan her health.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Talking to Benny privately over tea with the job sheet and a real question; it uncovered the fear of the software without shaming him.

qa.q: What might Benny have felt when shown the job sheet?
qa.a: Benny was embarrassed, since he went red, but perhaps relieved to finally admit being scared of the software.

grounding: Shows a young manager who notices one person carrying the load while another coasts, and resolves it through a fair, private conversation.

passage:
Team coach's note, week 3 of the app redesign.
Before work began, Sachin put a blank sheet on the wall and said, "On the last project, three of us were angry by week six and nobody said so. Let's decide now what fair looks like."
Vaibhav suggested each person take two tickets a week and flag early if they'll miss one. Nidhi added that design reviews count as work too, which nobody had thought of. Kabir asked what happens if someone's ill; they agreed the team reshuffles, no blame. The tracker is a column of names and ticks.
Three weeks in, Kabir flagged a missed ticket on Tuesday, not Friday, and Nidhi picked it up without a sigh. Stand-ups are calmer than anything I've seen on this floor all year.
What I did next: I asked Sachin to show the sheet to the other two teams.

qa.q: How many tickets a week did Vaibhav suggest each person take?
qa.a: Two tickets a week.

qa.q: What feeling seems to push Sachin to start the discussion?
qa.a: Sachin seems wary and a little tired of old resentment, remembering three people angry and silent by week six last time.

qa.q: Why does agreeing on fairness before the work starts help?
qa.a: Everyone knows the rules in advance, so a missed ticket is flagged early and handled by agreement instead of building quiet anger.

qa.q: How might Nidhi experience covering Kabir's missed ticket?
qa.a: Nidhi seems calm about it, probably because the rule was agreed openly and it doesn't feel like being taken advantage of 🙂

grounding: Shows a team openly agreeing what fair effort means at the start and tracking it simply, which prevents slow-building resentment.

passage:
At the play school, Rekha aunty tied red ribbons on half the children and yellow on the rest, just for relay teams.
By snack time, Anjali, a red ribbon on her wrist, had decided things. "Reds sit here. Yellows are slow." She pulled Tia away from Mira, a yellow, whom she had played with all week. "She's yellow," Anjali said, as if that explained everything.
Rekha aunty knelt down. "Yesterday you and Mira were best at swings. Is Mira different now?"
Anjali looked at her ribbon, then at Mira, and frowned.

qa.q: What colour ribbon was on Anjali's wrist?
qa.a: A red ribbon.

qa.q: What does Anjali's frown at the end suggest?
qa.a: Anjali seems puzzled and unsure, starting to notice that a ribbon made her treat a friend differently.

qa.q: How did Rekha aunty help Anjali think again?
qa.a: She knelt down and asked a gentle question about Mira and the swings, instead of scolding.

qa.q: What was snack time like for Mira?
qa.a: Mira probably felt hurt and confused when her playmate suddenly called her "yellow" and pulled Tia away.

grounding: Shows young children given meaningless coloured groups quickly favouring their own side and dismissing the other.

passage:
Monday: House teams were announced. Parul was in Blue House, and by lunch she was chanting "Blue, blue, we'll beat you!" at the Green table. Her friend Vidya was Green. "Greens are so slow," Parul joked. Vidya laughed, a little.
Thursday: At relay practice, Parul cheered only for Blue. When a Green runner tripped, the Blue kids laughed. Parul laughed too, then saw it was Vidya, picking gravel from her knee. Vidya didn't look at her.
Saturday: In the final relay, Vidya ran last for Green and overtook Blue to win. Blue groaned. Parul was quiet for a moment, then walked over. "That was fast. Is your knee okay?"
Vidya grinned. "Still sore. But I won."

qa.q: Which house was Parul in?
qa.a: Parul was in Blue House.

qa.q: What did Parul feel when she saw it was Vidya who had tripped?
qa.a: Parul felt a jolt of guilt and discomfort, realising she had laughed at her own friend just because of a house colour.

qa.q: How could Parul cheer for Blue without putting Green down?
qa.a: She could shout for her own runners and still clap for good running on any side, like she finally did on Saturday.

qa.q: What was Thursday like for Vidya?
qa.a: Vidya was hurt twice, by the fall and by her friend laughing, which is why she wouldn't look at Parul.

grounding: Shows a child cheering only for her own house and making the rival side seem lesser, until it touches a friend.

subtype: Left out for being from elsewhere [Receiver]
passage:
Yash, worried about the new school? Let your Lavanya paati tell you something.
When I was nine, my father's job moved us from Bhopal to Coimbatore. I spoke no Tamil. On my first day, the girls already had their hopscotch groups and tiffin circles. Every recess I stood near the water tap, washing my hands again and again. I watched everything, but I felt like a ghost. Nobody was cruel. That was the strange part. They just didn't see me.
On the eighth day, a girl called Kamala walked over with half a murukku and said something I didn't understand. Then she held up her fingers. "Onnu, rendu, moonu." One, two, three. She pulled me to the hopscotch squares.
I still remember how warm that murukku was.

qa.q: Where did Lavanya stand every recess?
qa.a: Near the water tap.

qa.q: How did young Lavanya feel during the first week?
qa.a: She felt invisible and lonely, "like a ghost", watching every group closely while nobody noticed her.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed things, and why did it work?
qa.a: Kamala offered food and taught numbers through a game, which let Lavanya join in without needing Tamil first.

qa.q: Why might Kamala have walked over on the eighth day?
qa.a: Kamala may have noticed the new girl alone at the tap every day and felt kind or curious enough to try, even without a shared language.

grounding: Shows a new child from another city and language finding groups already formed, feeling watchful and invisible until one kind gesture.

passage:
The school bus coughed and died on the flyover, forty minutes from home, in the June heat. The driver phoned for help: the Sector 9 school's bus would pick them up on its route.
"Great," Thomas announced. "Now we ride with the Sector 9 lot. Hold your bags, that lot all steal." The back rows laughed. Saurabh added, "And they can't even speak properly." More laughter. Thomas felt the warm buzz of it, everyone looking at him.
When the other bus arrived, the kids inside shuffled over without a word to make room. A boy in a faded blue uniform lifted Saurabh's cricket kit onto the rack for him. Nobody said thank you.
By evening, "Sector 9 steals" was a running joke in the class chat. Thomas had never been to Sector 9. He didn't know a single person from there. He hadn't thought about that.

qa.q: Where did the school bus break down?
qa.a: On the flyover, forty minutes from home.

qa.q: Why did Thomas keep joking about the Sector 9 kids?
qa.a: Thomas enjoyed the warm buzz of the group laughing and looking at him; the approval felt so good that he never questioned the label.

qa.q: What could Thomas ask himself before a joke like that next time?
qa.a: Whether he actually knows anyone from the group, and whether he would say it to the boy who lifted Saurabh's kit.

qa.q: What was it like for the Sector 9 kids to make room for the stranded students?
qa.a: They helped quietly, even lifting a kit, yet got no thanks and were being called thieves behind their backs.

grounding: Shows a teenager labelling kids from another school with sweeping stereotypes, rewarded by group laughter so the label spreads unexamined.

passage:
"Why aren't you coming to Kunal's sleepover? The whole group's going."
"Wasn't invited, Shreya."
"What? You sit with them every lunch."
"Arjun told me. Kunal's parents said 'not that one.' Because of my name. You know why."
"Rafiq, that's..."
"It's fine." He picked at his sandwich. "Maybe I'll just be Raf from now on. Nobody asks what Raf is."
"You'd change your name?"
"I'm so angry I could throw this tray. And then I feel stupid, like I'm the problem."
"You're not the problem. Come with me to Mrs Fernandes after lunch. Just so someone knows."
In the staffroom, Mrs Fernandes listened to all of it. "Thank you for telling me, Rafiq. This is not your fault, and your name is yours to keep. I'll speak to your class teacher today about how the group is treating you, and I'd like to call your parents this evening, if that's alright."

qa.q: What name does Rafiq say he might use from now on?
qa.a: Raf.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Rafiq describe?
qa.a: He feels angry enough to throw the tray and then ashamed, as if he were the problem.

qa.q: What did Mrs Fernandes's response get right?
qa.a: She thanked him, said it was not his fault, affirmed his name, and acted the same day with his class teacher and parents.

qa.q: How does Shreya see Rafiq's idea of changing his name?
qa.a: Shreya is shocked and upset; to her Rafiq is not the problem, so she brings him to a teacher right away.

grounding: Shows a teenager left out because of his religious identity, feeling anger, shame and a wish to hide who he is to be accepted.

subtype: Meeting the individual behind the label [Response]
passage:
For years the boys of Khedi and Pipariya had called each other names across the river. Khedi said Pipariya boys were thieves; Pipariya said Khedi boys were show-offs. Vijay had never spoken to one.
Then the block school merged the two kabaddi squads for the district tournament, and the coach put Vijay beside Manoj from Pipariya on the left flank. The first week they barely looked at each other. Manoj tackled late; Vijay muttered under his breath.
In the quarter-final at Sehore, Manoj held the raider's ankle just long enough for Vijay to lock him. They won by one point. On the tractor-trolley ride home, Manoj shared his roasted chana, and Vijay learned he wanted to be a vet, like Vijay's own cousin.
Back in Khedi, when his friend Raju started on "those Pipariya thieves", Vijay said, "Manoj isn't. Say something else."

qa.q: By how many points did they win the quarter-final?
qa.a: By one point.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel about Manoj in the first week?
qa.a: Vijay was wary and irritated, muttering at Manoj's late tackles, because Manoj was still just a boy from the other village.

qa.q: What changed Vijay's view, and what could others learn from it?
qa.a: Working toward the same win, then talking on the ride home; a shared goal turns a label into a person.

qa.q: How might Raju react to Vijay's reply?
qa.a: Raju may be surprised or a bit put out, since Vijay used to share the joke, but now the label has a real face.

grounding: Shows a teenager getting to know a boy from a disliked rival village through a shared sporting goal, which softens the old label.

passage:
Tuesday: In the hostel common room, Rekha found the kettle crusted and cups piled in the sink. "Classic C-wing," she told Mohit and Anu. "That whole wing is careless."
Friday: The kettle was crusted again. This time Anu had seen who did it: Priya, from Rekha's own A-wing. "Oh, Priya's had three exams this week," Rekha said. "She's just stressed. It's a one-off."
Sunday: Mohit, washing cups, said lightly, "So when C-wing does it, it's the wing, and when Priya does it, it's the exams?"
Rekha laughed. "That's different. You don't know Priya." She went back to her phone and didn't notice Mohit and Anu exchange a look.

qa.q: Who from A-wing left the kettle crusted on Friday?
qa.a: Priya, from Rekha's own A-wing.

qa.q: Why did Rekha excuse Priya so easily?
qa.a: Rekha felt protective and loyal toward someone from her own wing, so Priya's mess seemed like a stressed one-off.

qa.q: What question could Rekha ask herself before blaming a whole group next time?
qa.a: Whether she would say the same about her own wing if one of them did it, or whether she even knows who did it.

qa.q: How might the C-wing students feel if they heard Rekha on Tuesday?
qa.a: They would likely feel unfairly judged and annoyed, blamed as a whole wing for what one unknown person did.

grounding: Shows a young adult excusing a mess by her own wing as a one-off while blaming another wing's similar mess on the whole group, without noticing.
